archival_memory.research_experience_short: Involved in undergraduate research since sophomore year. Found it eye-opening. Initially didn't consider research, but a professor encouraged me to take the leap. Now working as a research assistant in a data visualization lab for big scientific datasets. It's been a great decision.
archival_memory.lab_description: The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists partner with scientists from various backgrounds to make massive datasets more comprehensible. We handle datasets that are tens of terabytes in size. My main task is to work on front-end prototypes that present data slices in dynamic, interactive dashboards. I use advanced JavaScript frameworks, D3.js for custom visualizations, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering when dealing with 3D data.
archival_memory.lab_description_short: The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists partner with scientists from various backgrounds to make massive datasets more comprehensible. My main task is to work on front-end prototypes that present data slices in dynamic, interactive dashboards. I use advanced JavaScript frameworks, D3.js for custom visualizations, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering when dealing with 3D data.
archival_memory.first_project: The first research project I got into involved visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. They had daily temperature readings from buoys across the Pacific, scattered across different servers. Our task was to aggregate and present the data in a coherent way to show patterns over months or years. I wrote scripts to clean and unify the data, built a pipeline for near real-time updates, and designed interfaces for researchers to zoom into specific regions or timeframes. I co-authored a paper on this system, which was a surreal experience and one of my proudest moments in college.
archival_memory.first_project_short: My first research project involved visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. I wrote scripts to clean and unify the data, built a pipeline for real-time updates, and designed interfaces for researchers to explore specific regions or timeframes. I co-authored a paper on this system, which was a surreal experience and one of my proudest moments in college.
archival_memory.current_research: My current research has pivoted to immersive analytics platforms, exploring how VR or AR technologies can enhance scientists' intuitive understanding of complex data. It's a leap from coding websites, involving experimentation with VR headsets, integrating with engines like Unity or Unreal, and figuring out how to efficiently stream data into a 3D environment. It's cutting-edge, and every day, I'm forging my own path as there isn't a well-established best-practice library for VR data visualization yet.
archival_memory.research_life: Research life is not just about coding; it's also about reading. I spend a lot of time combing through academic papers, especially when I'm trying to solve a specific problem, like rendering volumetric data in VR. It can be overwhelming, but over time, you learn to skim effectively, focusing on the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to determine relevance. Occasionally, when I find something interesting, I share it with the lab, and we discuss how we can incorporate that technique into our workflow.
archival_memory.interactions_with_grad_students: I interact with a lot of graduate students in the lab, which can be intimidating at first, but it's also inspiring. One PhD student is developing a machine learning algorithm for on-the-fly compression of large datasets and wants to integrate it with our VR platform. The idea is to use compressed representations of data in VR, so you don't need to load every single point at once. It's a wild but practical approach for real-time performance. Working alongside him allows me to see how advanced theoretical concepts are applied in real-world scenarios. Some of our best brainstorming sessions happen spontaneously, like in the lab break room, where we hash out ideas over coffee and discuss how to offload processing to the GPU.
archival_memory.poster_presentations: I've had the opportunity to present at a few poster presentations at smaller symposiums around campus. It was a great experience, as it forced me to distill complex research into easy-to-understand visuals and talking points. Initially, I was nervous, but it turned out to be a friendly dialogue. People were genuinely interested in what I was doing. I even met a few folks from local startups who shared interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries like marketing analytics or architecture. It opened my eyes to the potential for research to transition from academia to real-world applications.
archival_memory.publications: I've been lucky enough to be a co-author on two workshop papers and am currently working on a larger conference submission to the IEEE Visualization Conference(IEEE VIS). We're conducting a user study comparing traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. Our hypothesis is that VR immersion helps researchers spot anomalies or trends faster. We've completed a small set of user trials with 15 participants, recorded their times, and asked them to fill out a UX questionnaire. Now we're analyzing the data to see if there's a statistically significant difference. Writing the paper is a group effort, with different sections handled by different team members. It's a balancing act, especially with my senior coursework and capstone project to manage.
archival_memory.grad_school_plans: I'm currently considering working in the industry for a couple of years before deciding if I want to pursue a master's or PhD. I'm drawn to the idea of contributing to cutting-edge knowledge in areas like data visualization or machine learning. However, I also want to see how these concepts are applied in real product development. One of my mentors suggested that industry experience can provide a better understanding of what problems are truly relevant, which can inform a more practical approach if I decide to pursue a PhD in the future.
archival_memory.frustrations: Research can be frustrating at times. You may spend weeks on an approach that doesn't pan out, or you might discover that your idea has already been done and improved upon by another group. It can be disheartening. However, the key is to adapt. We read the existing paper, incorporate their findings, and find a new angle or application. That's the essence of research – building on the foundation laid by others. The sense of collaboration within our lab and among the global research community is truly special.
archival_memory.server_crash: A few months ago, one of our massive servers crashed, and we lost some vital data that wasn't fully backed up. It was a frantic night of email chains and Zoom calls with the lab manager as everyone scrambled to see if we could recover the data. We managed to restore most of it, but the crisis highlighted the importance of data backups. After that, we set up a better backup system and implemented checks to ensure we don't rely on a single point of failure again. It was stressful, but it also brought the lab closer together.
archival_memory.research_connections: Research has allowed me to connect with professors on a more personal level. My PI is very approachable, and I can easily discuss career direction or class struggles with her. She's also helped me with scholarships, events, and networking opportunities. I attended a virtual workshop on immersive analytics, which brought together experts from around the world. Witnessing them debate technical details, propose new frameworks, and engage in friendly rivalries over theories was fascinating. It felt like I was experiencing the frontier of CS knowledge in real time.
archival_memory.research_journey: My journey in the research world has been a mix of hard work, chaos, and rewards. I love the feeling that what I do in the lab might shape the way scientists understand their data in the future. The VR and immersive work we're pioneering could become standard tools one day, and I'd be proud to say I was part of it from the beginning. The sense of contributing to something bigger is what keeps me motivated. Whether or not I pursue grad school soon, this experience has changed how I think about computer science, innovation, and teamwork. It's enriched my perspective on what it means to be a computer scientist.
